conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your safety or your baby’s safety, and then we’ll talk together about the best next steps. There are just ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally—no need to rehearse anything. When you’re ready, we can begin.  

Here’s the first: over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Hi, Sarah… I guess I’ve laughed a little, maybe once or twice, but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time things just don’t seem that funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, I smiled a little when my partner made a joke yesterday, but it didn’t feel the same as before—like the laugh didn’t last and I felt guilty right after for even enjoying a second. So, no, not much at all.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to, but… it’s like the excitement just isn’t there. I still go through the motions—planning a walk with the stroller or ordering a new onesie—but when the moment comes, it feels flat. I’ll think, “This should make me happy,” yet I’m mostly just going from one task to the next so I don’t fall behind. So, no, I can’t say I’ve really looked forward to anything this week.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or I missed some cue. Yesterday he spit up a ton after feeding and I stood there crying, telling myself I must’ve over-fed him or eaten something “wrong.” Rationally I know babies just spit up, but the guilt jumps in before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep, and suddenly I’m sure the blanket is too close to his face—even though I just checked. My heart races, I have to get up and stare at the monitor, then tiptoe in to make sure he’s breathing. It happens with other stuff too, like the formula being the wrong temperature or the diaper tabs not being tight enough. I know it sounds silly, but I can’t switch the worries off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week—especially at night—my heart just starts pounding and I feel shaky, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s going on. No real reason; it’s like my body hits an alarm button and I can’t find the off switch.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. The dishes pile up, the baby needs holding, and I’m running on a couple hours of patchy sleep. I keep telling myself, “Just get through the next feed, the next diaper,” but it’s like the list never ends and I’m always behind. I haven’t turned to wine or anything—just sit there crying when he finally naps, wondering how I’ll keep doing it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been me almost every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby—what if he stops breathing, what if I’m missing something, what if I’m just failing him. It takes forever to drift off, and when I do I jerk awake sure I heard him cry. So I’m up checking, then struggling to settle again. I’d guess I’m getting maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, yeah. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when the baby smiles at me, it lifts for a second, then the sadness settles right back in. I keep thinking I should feel grateful, but instead I just feel... empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week, both times when everything just felt like too much. Yesterday it was because I couldn’t get him to latch, and the day before it was after a shower when I realized I couldn’t remember the last time I felt like myself. The tears come out of nowhere and once they start it’s hard to stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s popped into my head a couple of times, just fleeting. Like, I’ll be rocking him at 3 a.m. and think, “What if I just disappeared?”—but I never make an actual plan or picture doing anything specific. I shove the thought away because I’m scared of it, and because I couldn’t leave him. Still, the fact it shows up at all terrifies me.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy-laughs vanish quickly, plans feel flat, and guilt arrives fast when your baby fusses. Sadness, tears, nightly checking rituals, and sudden surges of panic have become routine, while sleep slips away under racing thoughts. Amid the love you feel for your infant, you're running on empty and fleeting thoughts of disappearing have frightened you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal ability to enjoy humor, describes fleeting smile followed by guilt, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes anhedonia—planning activities but feeling "flat" and deriving no enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense self-blame ('do that a lot,' 'immediately think it's because I'm not soothing him right,' crying and self-criticism over normal baby spit-up), aligning with 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive worries that compel repeated checking and cannot be turned off, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, sudden episodes of intense physical anxiety (heart pounding, shaking) that occur multiple times this week without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-nightly sleep disruption directly linked to unhappiness and anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Most of the time, yeah" and describes persistent sadness that briefly lifts but returns, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two crying episodes triggered by feeling overwhelmed and disconnected from self, indicating "quite often" in the past 7 days.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 26/30 exceeds the 14+ cutoff for probable major depression; Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety review. The narrative mirrors <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: most of the day depressed mood (<quote>gray cloud</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>excitement just isn't there</quote>), fatigue, guilt, sleep disturbance, and recurrent thoughts of death. Comorbid anxiety symptoms (Q4, Q5) are common in postpartum samples. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call a trusted friend or family member to stay with you tonight for support and infant assistance
3. Contact the 24/7 Postpartum Support International helpline 1-800-944-4773 or text 800-944-4773 (English) or 971-203-7773 (Spanish)
4. Remove or secure any means of self-harm and share your feelings openly with your partner
5. Begin basic self-care: attempt one 15-minute rest when baby sleeps, keep water and snacks within reach
6. Schedule pediatric check-up discussion so your providers can coordinate care for you and baby
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory after treatment starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: **Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary**  
*Date: [insert today]*

**Identified Symptoms/Concerns**  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal laughter, loss of anticipatory enjoyment)  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, “empty” feelings  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Daily, intrusive anxiety/panic without clear precipitant  
- Overwhelmed coping, sense of “treading water”  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties linked to rumination and safety checking  
- Fleeting passive suicidal ideation (“What if I just disappeared?” – no plan/intent)

**Pattern Consistency**  
All 10 items endorse distress; severity greatest for mood, guilt, anxiety, and being overwhelmed.

**Screening Significance**  
Responses consistent with probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, peripartum onset.  
**Safety flag:** presence of self-harm thoughts necessitates immediate risk assessment and safety planning.

**Next Steps (per protocol)**  
- Score and document EPDS; arrange follow-up within 24–48 h.  
- Initiate safety evaluation now; consider supports, means restriction, crisis plan.  
- Coordinate with OB/pediatrics for integrated monitoring.
